The numbers 1, 2, ..., 2100 are written on a board. Every second, Mark takes two numbers on the board, \( a \) and \( b \), erases them, and replaces them with \( \gcd(a, b) \) and \( \operatorname{lcm}(a, b) \). Mark stops once any move he makes will not change the numbers written on the board. Compute the number of divisors of the 2026th smallest positive integer written on the board when he finishes.

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let \(N=2100\).

For each prime \(p\), the multiset of \(p\)-adic valuations on the board is invariant, since

\[
v_p(\gcd(a,b))=\min(v_p(a),v_p(b)),\qquad
v_p(\operatorname{lcm}(a,b))=\max(v_p(a),v_p(b)).
\]

When Mark stops, no move can change the board. For a pair \(a,b\), this means

\[
\{a,b\}=\{\gcd(a,b),\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\},
\]

which happens exactly when one of \(a,b\) divides the other. Thus the final numbers form a divisibility chain. Sorting them increasingly as

\[
x_1\mid x_2\mid \cdots \mid x_{2100},
\]

the exponent of each prime in \(x_i\) must be the \(i\)-th smallest \(p\)-adic valuation among the original numbers \(1,2,\dots,2100\).

We need \(x_{2026}\). There are

\[
2100-2026+1=75
\]

numbers from \(x_{2026}\) through \(x_{2100}\). For a prime \(p\), the exponent of \(p\) in \(x_{2026}\) is at least \(r\) if at least \(75\) of the original numbers are divisible by \(p^r\). Hence the exponent is the largest \(r\) such that

\[
\left\lfloor \frac{2100}{p^r}\right\rfloor \ge 75.
\]

Since \(2100=75\cdot 28\), this is equivalent to

\[
p^r\le 28.
\]

Therefore

\[
x_{2026}=\operatorname{lcm}(1,2,\dots,28).
\]

The prime factorization is

\[
x_{2026}=2^4\cdot 3^3\cdot 5^2\cdot 7\cdot 11\cdot 13\cdot 17\cdot 19\cdot 23.
\]

Thus the number of positive divisors is

\[
(4+1)(3+1)(2+1)(1+1)^6
=5\cdot 4\cdot 3\cdot 64
=3840.
\]

\[
\boxed{3840}
\]
